title: AI in Education #14: Five Things I Learned from Manu Kapur about productive failure
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton, who spent a decade building failure into his maths lessons and then renounced the practice in favor of explicit instruction, uses a conversation with learning scientist Manu Kapur to revisit that choice. The piece distinguishes Kapur's precisely defined productive failure from the looser notion of productive struggle, and lays out the four mechanisms Kapur credits: activation, awareness, affect and assembly. Barton stresses that failure only becomes productive when a teacher skillfully assembles student attempts against the expert solution. The article then turns practical, describing Kapur's short intuition-building protocol and longer invention protocol, and it stages a genuine debate with the faultless-communication school by contrasting diagnostic and prospective prior knowledge. It closes by applying Kapur's distinction between a learning zone and a performance zone to AI tutors, arguing that a tutor that can be coaxed into giving the answer undermines learning and that AI might be more useful before instruction than after it.
points: Kapur separates productive failure, where the end state of a designed problem is not reached, from productive struggle, which he says has no boundary and so cannot be designed or studied.
Failure pays off only through assembly: the teacher gathers student attempts, presents them without embarrassment, and compares their features with the expert solution.
The intuition-building protocol uses 20 to 30 quick contrasting-case questions in ten minutes, giving students early success rates of up to 60 percent before any teaching.
Kapur answers direct-instruction advocates by pointing to prospective priors, the intuitive knowledge students already hold about a concept they have never been taught.

An AI tutor that can be persuaded to hand over the answer should not be used for learning, and Kapur's lab is training models on productive failure principles to work with students before instruction.
quotes: For the first 10 years of my teaching career, I made sure my lessons included lots of student failure. Whenever I introduced a new idea, my students had to wrestle with it first, even though they had little hope of figuring out the answer. They had to struggle, and usually fail, before I felt I was allowed to show them the proper way to do it. I thought I was a brilliant teacher. My students’ pained expressions suggested otherwise.

Manu is clear that they are not the same thing. Productive struggle is something people experience and describe, but ask ten people to define it and you will get ten different answers. There is no boundary to it, which means you cannot design for it, and you certainly cannot study it.
The idea behind it is simple. We all believe we can learn from our mistakes. So, as Manu asks, if failure is such a good teacher, why do we wait for it to happen? Why not design for it deliberately?

Assembly is where a teacher, tutor or resource brings it all together, comparing the students’ ideas with the expert solution. It is in that contrast that students start to see the deep structure: why my method did not work, and why this one does.

Manu’s answer was to always start with intuition building. Before they have learnt the concept, students get success rates of up to 60% on these items. Share that back with them - you haven’t been taught this yet, but your intuitions are pretty good - and it is motivating.

Both approaches agree that students learn by using prior knowledge, and that a problem they have no way into carries a heavy cognitive load. The difference is what you do next. One response is: they can’t solve it, so they don’t know anything, so tell them. The other is: they can’t solve it, so let’s redesign the problem so it activates what they do know, even if some of that is wrong, and use it as the basis to teach.

If a student hands a productive failure problem to an AI tutor and gets the right answer, their performance looks great, but they haven’t learnt much. A tutor that can be persuaded to hand over the answer, he says, should not be used for learning.
And he doesn’t assume students know how to learn with AI. When he asks adults when they last used an AI tutor to learn something new all the way to mastery, the answer is almost never.
